p1.key: Gas particles are far apart, so gases have low densities. Because of the large spaces between particles they expand to fill any container, diffuse readily and are easily compressed.

At 460 K both cyclooctane (b.p. 421 K) and cyclononane (444 K) are gases, and gases mix most easily because their particles move fast and freely. In each of the other pairs at least one compound is a liquid at the stated temperature.
p1.flag: old-style question; answer inferred (gases mix most readily)

p1.key: On melting, the molecules gain freedom to move past each other (I). Water is unusual: the open hydrogen-bonded lattice of ice collapses, so liquid water is denser and the molecules are on average closer together, so II is false.
p1.flag: relies on the density anomaly of ice

p1.key: The vapour is richer in the more volatile component. Propan-2-ol has the lower boiling point, so the first vapour contains a higher fraction of propan-2-ol but is not pure. Fractional distillation separates them gradually.
For 10 g: heating the solid from 10 to 30 °C takes 400 J, and melting (the plateau from 400 to 1200 J) takes 800 J. For 20 g, double both: 800 + 1600 = 2400 J.
Freezing is exothermic: as forces form between particles, energy is released and the particles take up fixed, more ordered positions. Particle size never changes.
During boiling, the energy supplied is used to overcome intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) so molecules can separate into the gas, not to raise kinetic energy. Covalent O–H bonds are not broken.
Average kinetic energy of particles is directly proportional to absolute (Kelvin) temperature, so the graph is a straight line through the origin (D).
Average kinetic energy depends only on absolute temperature, not on the identity or amount of the gas. All three are at 298 K, so the ratio is 1 : 1 : 1.

Vapour pressure increases with temperature, and increasingly steeply, because the fraction of molecules with enough energy to escape grows exponentially (graph D). It never decreases with temperature.
p1.flag: Vapour pressure curves are not explicit in the 2025 guide.

p1.key: At any temperature, particles have a range of kinetic energies (Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution); temperature relates to the average energy. So C is the incorrect statement.
As temperature rises, a growing fraction of molecules have enough energy to escape the liquid, so vapour pressure increases more and more steeply: exponentially, not linearly.

p1.key: The average kinetic energy of gas particles is directly proportional to the absolute (Kelvin) temperature, so the graph is a straight line through the origin.

Vapour pressure depends only on temperature (and the identity of the liquid). Raising T gives more molecules enough energy to escape the liquid. Surface area and the amount of liquid or vapour do not change the equilibrium vapour pressure.

p1.key: Sublimation is a direct change from solid to gas without melting: HgCl<sub>2</sub>(s) → HgCl<sub>2</sub>(g). C is the reverse (deposition); A and D are chemical reactions.

A mixture can contain elements and/or compounds (I), and each component keeps its own properties (III), which is why mixtures can be separated physically. Components need not be in the same phase (e.g. sand in water), so II is false.

A heterogeneous mixture has non-uniform composition with visibly separate phases. Diagram A shows gas particles above a separate solid layer of a different substance. B is a uniform gaseous mixture (homogeneous), C is a pure gaseous element and D is a single solid phase.
